column2: A thousand fish are caught, marked, and let go. A while later, a second net catches a thousand. Of those, a hundred are marked.
Now look at all the fish no net ever touched.
Our best guess for this dark cell is eight thousand one hundred. And we can say how sure we are.
Why not count one patch and scale up? This net covers one hundredth of the lake. Four hundred fifty-one fish, times a hundred, is forty-five thousand one hundred.
Try two other spots. Same answer?
Not even close. In the weeds, eighty-eight thousand. In open water, only two thousand eight hundred.
The net knows it covered a hundredth of the water. It can't know what share of the fish that was.
In nineteen fifty, the probabilist William Feller put this puzzle in his famous textbook. Others had been using it for years, and his first edition never mentions them.
Feller marked his fish with red spots. Ours glow, so you can see them.
Read the catch one way first. Of the thousand marked fish, the second net caught a hundred. One in ten.
So guess that the second net caught about one in ten of all the fish. It caught a thousand. A thousand is one tenth of how many?
Ten thousand. The marked fish have measured our net for us. It searched about a tenth of the fish.
Read the same fact the other way. One fish in ten in the second catch is marked, so about one in ten in the lake is. We marked a thousand, so the lake holds about ten times that.
Marked times second catch, over caught twice. A thousand times a thousand, over a hundred. Ten thousand. Call it the soup guess.
Why should that work? How sure can we be? And when does it fail?
Stir soup, and one spoonful tells you how salty the whole pot is. Our second catch is the spoonful.
We built this lake, so we can peek. We marked the first thousand near the dock, and let them go there.
Watch them swim. Will the marks stay bunched up near the dock?
The fish stay crowded where they like to be. But the marks spread out evenly among them.
Wherever the second net goes, about one fish in ten it catches is marked. The catch is a small copy of the lake's mix.

The fullest corner has twenty-eight hundred eleven fish, two hundred eighty-two marked, and the emptiest has two hundred four, twenty-five marked. Both sit near one in every ten, and the small one wobbles more.
Mixing is what makes the table fair. Being marked becomes unrelated to where a fish swims. In both columns, the second net takes the same one in ten, so the line across the table runs straight.
That's what independent means here. The second net doesn't care which fish were caught before, as long as every fish is as easy to catch.
To see exactly why, shrink the lake. Twenty fish, five of them marked. And our net holds four.
Random means every group of four is equally likely. How many groups are there?

Twenty choices for the first fish, nineteen for the second, then eighteen, then seventeen. But the same four fish come out in twenty-four orders, four times three times two times one, and that's still one netful. So divide by twenty-four. Four thousand eight hundred forty-five.
Sort them by how many marked fish they hold. Which pile is biggest?
One marked fish. One in four, same as the lake. The soup again.

Take the pile with two marked fish. Ten ways to pick two of the five marked ones. For each, a hundred and five ways to pick two of the fifteen unmarked ones, like shirts and pants. One thousand fifty.
Divide every pile by all four thousand eight hundred forty-five, and you get the chances. About twenty-eight percent, forty-seven, twenty-two, three, and under one.
Mathematicians call it the hypergeometric distribution. If we know the lake, we know the chances of every catch. But we only know the catch.
A new lake, and we don't know its size. Call it the mystery lake. We marked ten, caught ten, and three were marked.
Let's try the soup guess first. Ten times ten, over three?
About thirty-three. Now check it properly. What's the smallest the lake could be? We've already seen seventeen different fish.
For each possible lake size, ask how likely it is to see exactly three marked. A lake of twenty, about eight percent. Thirty-three, about thirty-two percent. Sixty, about sixteen.
Now sweep through every size.
The curve peaks at thirty-three, just as the soup guess said. It's called the likelihood. Think of it as a score for each lake size. How likely our catch would be, if the lake were that size.

Add up every height, out to lakes as big as you like, and you get about sixteen and two thirds. Real chances would add up to one, a hundred percent. The lake has one size, so these aren't chances that it's a certain size. They're scores for comparing guesses.
Here's every lake size and every possible count at once.
Cut across at one lake size. And what do you get?
The chances from counting each netful. They add to one.

Cut along at our three, and you get the score curve. Its heights, out to every lake size, add to sixteen and two thirds. Same mountains, two questions. What catch will this lake give, and which lake gave our catch?

Feller found the top score without drawing anything. Compare each lake size with the one just below it. Divide one score by the other, and almost everything cancels. That leftover fraction is also how code can walk the curve, one size at a time.

In the mystery lake, the step from thirty-two to thirty-three leaves twenty-three times twenty-three, over thirty-three times sixteen. That's five hundred twenty-nine against five hundred twenty-eight. The top one wins, so the score goes up. From thirty-three to thirty-four, it's five hundred seventy-six against five hundred seventy-eight, so it goes down.
So take the top minus the bottom, written with letters. Multiply it out. And what survives?
Marked times second catch, minus caught twice times lake size. In the mystery lake, ten times ten, minus three times thirty-three. One. While that's positive, the score is still rising.
Now write it with the table's four cells. It becomes first catch only times second catch only, minus caught twice times the dark cell.
In the mystery lake, seven times seven, minus three times sixteen. One, same as before. Back to Feller's lake.
So start with a small dark cell and let it grow. Where does the climb stop?
In each column, the green part is what the second net caught. While the green share in the unmarked column is bigger than in the marked column, the score keeps climbing.
A hundred times eight thousand one hundred is eight hundred ten thousand. So is nine hundred times nine hundred. The shares match, the line is straight, and the table balances.

A straight line is what two independent catches look like on average. So the size with the top score and the soup guess agree, rounded down to a whole fish, like thirty-three from thirty-three and a third.

At Feller's numbers the line goes exactly straight at ten thousand. So the step up from nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine changes nothing, and the two tie for the top score. Feller just says ten thousand.
Let's check this by cheating. Build a lake of exactly ten thousand fish, and run Feller's experiment on it ten thousand times.
Where do the counts of fish caught twice pile up?
They pile up in a bell around a hundred. Most land within about nine of it.

But the guess divides by that count, and division bends things. Ninety caught twice gives about eleven thousand one hundred. A hundred and ten gives about nine thousand one hundred. Ten too few pushes harder than ten too many.
Ninety-five percent of the guesses land from about eighty-five hundred to just over twelve thousand. Their average is about ten thousand and ninety, a little high.

Two lines of code run all the experiments. The last line checks their average against the exact one, built by the same rule as each netful. They agree, within the simulation's own wobble. Always check a simulation against something you can compute exactly.
With a smaller experiment it gets worse. In a lake of a thousand fish, mark fifty and catch fifty. How often does the second catch hold no marked fish at all?
About one time in fourteen. Then the soup guess divides by zero.

Chapman's fix is to add one to each count, and subtract one at the end, as if one imaginary fish had been caught both times. It never divides by zero. With none caught twice it still answers two thousand six hundred, a number, not an answer.

Here we expect only two and a half caught twice. Over the experiments that catch any, the soup guess runs about twenty-four percent high, and Chapman's runs about six and a half percent low. Once you expect four or more, its average lands within two percent of the truth, though any one guess still scatters widely.
So far the lake was known, and we watched the guesses scatter. Now turn it around. We don't know the lake. Which sizes could plausibly have given us our hundred caught twice?

Only nineteen hundred fish? Then the second net scooped up all nine hundred unmarked fish and only a hundred of the thousand marked ones. The chance of that is about five in a one followed by four hundred thirty zeros.
A million fish? Then we'd expect to catch about one marked fish, not a hundred.
Even at the best size, catching exactly a hundred had only about a four percent chance. Is that a problem?
Flip a hundred coins. Exactly fifty heads comes up only about eight percent of the time, yet it's the most likely count.
Now the careful range. For each lake size, ask whether a hundred caught twice would land in that lake's middle ninety-five percent. Keep the sizes where it would.
Build that range for every experiment. In the long run, it rings the true size at least ninety-five times in a hundred, whatever that size is. Like a ring toss.

Statisticians call it a ninety-five percent confidence interval. For Feller's catch it runs from about eighty-four hundred to about twelve thousand one hundred. Close to the range we watched when the lake was known, but a different question. There the lake was fixed and the catch moved. Here the catch is fixed, and we try every lake size.
What makes the range tight?

Mostly, more fish caught twice, which means marking more and catching more. Four times as many roughly halves the range. Catching a bigger share of the lake helps more and more, and when every fish is caught twice in this lake, the range shrinks to a single size.
Every failure breaks one rule. On average, the second catch must hold the same share of marked fish that the lake held on marking day.
Some fish are bold and easy to catch, both times. Will the guess be too big, or too small?

Too small. Bold fish land in the caught-twice cell more than their share, so the dark cell shrinks. If three fish in ten are three times as easy to catch, the guess comes out around seventy-seven fifty.
Fish that learn to love the bait do the same. Fish that learn to avoid it push the guess up.
If marks wash off, marked fish look unmarked. That pushes it up too.
Two thousand newcomers dilute the marks, so you count the lake at the second catch.
What if three fish out of ten die between the catches?
The guess doesn't move. Death doesn't care about marks, so the share stays one in ten. But it counts the lake on marking day, not the seven thousand left.
If the marks never mix, the answer depends on where you fish. Near the dock you'd say sixty-two fifty, on the far side twenty-five thousand.
Around eighteen hundred, the French mathematician Laplace used the same table to count France. Births were written down, so in our table, each newborn is a marked fish.

At his request, officials counted everyone in chosen towns across France. Just over two million people, with about seventy-two thousand births a year. That's one birth for every twenty-eight and a bit people. Taking France's births as a million a year, that's about twenty-eight point four million people.
It counts bugs as well. Say two reviewers read the same code without comparing notes. One finds thirty bugs, the other twenty-four, and twelve are the same. How many are still hiding?

Thirty times twenty-four, over twelve, is sixty. They found forty-two, so about eighteen are still hiding. But only twelve were caught twice, and that's not many. If every bug is equally easy to find, the careful range for all the bugs runs from forty-seven to ninety-four.

Reviewers of different skill cause no trouble. Bugs of different difficulty do. Bugs that are easy for both reviewers swell the caught-twice cell and pull the guess down, like the bold fish. So expect sixty, and the range, to run low.

And it has counted the dead. Between March and June of nineteen ninety-nine, in the war in Kosovo, four lists named about four thousand four hundred different victims between them. Together they make a table of sixteen cells, one for each mix of lists, and one cell holds the people on no list. From how the lists overlap, researchers estimated about ten thousand four hundred Kosovar Albanians killed in those months. With four lists, they could also allow for lists that lean on each other, which two catches can never do. Years later, a name-by-name count for the same months found nine thousand seven hundred ninety, inside their range.
France, the bugs, Kosovo. What do they share?
Each is a table with one cell nobody can see, filled in by the cells we can.
